title: Low Interoception: Why Your Body Goes Unheard #Shorts
description:
Low interoception is common in ADHD -- it means your brain has reduced ability to detect internal body signals like hunger, thirst, exhaustion, or even needing the bathroom. It explains why you can hyperfocus for five hours and forget you haven't eaten or moved. You're not ignoring your body; the signal isn't arriving the way it should.
Free 2-minute ADHD brain quiz: https://bloomfocus.org/quiz
Follow for daily ADHD content.

voiceover: Someone cancels plans and you feel like your whole day just collapsed. That's not being dramatic. ADHD brains have a broken emotional brake system. The prefrontal cortex, the part that softens emotional signals before they hit full force, has lower dopamine activity in ADHD. So feelings arrive unfiltered. Full volume. No buffer. A small rejection lands like a real rejection. A minor mistake replays for hours. This is called emotional dysregulation, and it's in the neurology, not your personality. Here's the twist: trying to logic your way out in the moment doesn't work, because the prefrontal cortex is already offline. Instead, name the emotion out loud before you react. One word, spoken or written. 'Shame.' 'Panic.' That single act routes the signal through language processing and slows the flood by about 90 seconds, just enough for your brake system to catch up. Follow for daily ADHD content.

description:
If you have ADHD, emotions don't just feel bigger — there's a neurological reason they arrive at full volume with no filter. This short breaks down the prefrontal cortex dopamine deficit behind emotional dysregulation and gives you one evidence-based technique to slow the flood before you react. voiceover: You pushed through for three weeks straight. Now you can't answer a single text. That's not laziness. That's ADHD burnout, and it has a specific cycle. ADHD brains run on dopamine-driven hyperfocus and adrenaline to compensate for low baseline drive. You can sprint, but the cost is invisible until it isn't. The crash hits your working memory first: you lose words mid-sentence. Then your emotional regulation drops out. Then even low-effort tasks feel like lifting concrete. Here's what makes it worse: resting feels like failing, so you push again before the tank refills, and the cycle tightens. The exit is not a productivity hack. It's three consecutive days of no output pressure, at least one sensory-easy activity, and sleep before 11pm. Not forever. Just enough to let dopamine stores actually rebuild. Follow for daily ADHD content.

title: The ADHD Burnout Cycle Nobody Warns You About #Shorts
description:
ADHD burnout is not regular tiredness — it follows a specific neurological cycle driven by dopamine depletion and adrenaline-based compensation, and pushing through only tightens the loop. This short names the real mechanism behind the crash and gives a concrete three-day reset protocol that works with ADHD wiring, not against it. Common in ADHD, especially in high-masking adults.
Free 2-minute ADHD brain quiz: https://bloomfocus.org/quiz
Follow for daily ADHD content.

voiceover: You can hyperfocus for six hours on a documentary about medieval siege weapons. But the email your boss needs? You have stared at it for four days and typed nothing. That is not laziness. That is your interest-based nervous system. Neurotypical brains run on importance and deadlines. ADHD brains run almost entirely on interest, novelty, urgency, and emotional pull. Low dopamine transporter density means your prefrontal cortex cannot manufacture motivation on command. It literally has to feel compelling or your brain will not release enough dopamine to fire the starter. So what do you do? Stop trying to make boring things feel important. Make them feel interesting instead. Read that email out loud in a ridiculous accent. Race yourself to a two-minute timer. Attach it to the song that always locks you in. You are not broken. You just need a different ignition. Follow for daily ADHD content.
